paras: The Tenderloin mob threat against John Brown occurred in the early morning of August 20, 1903, at Sixth Avenue and Thirtieth Street in New York City, when a street crowd cried for the lynching of Brown, a Black cabman, after he was charged with stabbing a white cabman, Michael Lynch. Police held Brown and stopped the crowd, and he was later held in $1,000 bail. New York papers headlined the lynching cries, and the story was reprinted in Savannah two weeks later.

Brown, 24, of West Twenty-seventh Street, and Lynch, 30, of West Thirty-first Street, were 'nighthawk' cabmen who waited for fares outside the Haymarket dance hall. According to the Tribune, Lynch beat Brown in a race for a man and woman leaving the Haymarket, and when Lynch returned hours later Brown accused him of unfair methods. The Evening World gave a different start, saying the two rushed for the same couple and that Lynch 'took offense at Brown, who is a colored man.'

The men came to blows in the gutter opposite Frank Moran's saloon, a block from the West Thirtieth Street police station, and Lynch was getting the better of the fight. In the Commercial-Advertiser's version, onlookers from nearby resorts cheered, and cries of 'Do the nigger up!' were frequent. Brown was then charged with drawing a pocket knife and stabbing Lynch fourteen times in the abdomen.

A patrolman, whose name the papers spelled Busweiller, Buseellier and Ruseelier, ran from the station on hearing Lynch's cries. He said he had to club Brown before Brown would release his hold on Lynch, and it took several policemen to get Brown to a cell. Several men in the crowd, which the Herald and Tribune put at about two hundred, began to shout 'Lynch the nigger!' The Evening World described a crowd of 'half a hundred men' that rushed Brown once he was disarmed, crying 'Lynch him! Kill him!', and said the reserves fought it off with clubs, helped when the arriving ambulance drew the crowd's attention. Dr. Thorne of New York Hospital took Lynch away and said he would probably die.

Brown refused to make a statement and was arraigned in the Jefferson Market Police Court before Magistrate Breen, who held him in $1,000 bail for examination the following Saturday. No arrests of anyone in the crowd were reported. No later report of Lynch's death or recovery, of the examination or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The Evening World ran the story the same afternoon under 'Mob Fights to Lynch Stabber' and 'Police Reserves Use Clubs in Defense of Negro,' while calling Brown a 'Maddened Black' and noting witnesses who said he acted in self-defense. The next morning the Tribune led with 'Negro Stabs 14 Times' over a deck reading 'Cries of "Lynch the Nigger!"', qualifying the stabbing with 'it is charged' and 'it is alleged.' The Herald gave it a short item about a cabmen's fight over a 'fare,' mentioning the lynching cries in one sentence.

On September 5 the Savannah Morning News reprinted the Commercial-Advertiser's account under 'Street Row Near Police,' keeping both slur-laden cries and the arraignment. No coverage in the Black press was found.

The accounts differ on how far the crowd went: only the Evening World reported a rush at Brown and a fight with the reserves, while the Herald and Tribune said the arrival of more police ended the shouts and the crowd dispersed. They also differ on the crowd's size and on who provoked the fight, with the Evening World recording witnesses on both sides.

reader.title: Tenderloin mob threat against John Brown (1903)
bases: After John Brown, a Black cabman, stabbed white cabman Michael Lynch, a crowd cried 'Lynch him! Kill him!' and 'Lynch the nigger!' and, by one account, rushed police holding Brown before being fought off or dispersed; the officer's clubbing of Brown during the arrest is secondary (A1, A2, A3, A4).

Two independently written New York reports (A1, A2) and the Commercial-Advertiser text (A3, reprinted in A4) agree that a crowd cried for Brown's lynching after the stabbing and that police stopped it (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Evening World report
accounts.gist: Lynch took offense at Brown, 'a colored man,' in a rush for the same fare; Brown, getting the worst of the fight, drew a knife; after police disarmed him, a crowd of about fifty rushed him crying 'Lynch him! Kill him!' and reserves fought it off. Witnesses split on who provoked the fight.

accounts.label: Commercial-Advertiser / Tribune report
accounts.gist: Lynch won a race for a fare hours earlier; when he returned Brown accused him of unfair methods, and Brown, losing the fight, allegedly stabbed him; the patrolman says he had to club Brown to make him release Lynch; shouts of 'Lynch the nigger!' from about 200 onlookers were stopped by arriving police.

accounts.label: Herald report
accounts.gist: About 200 people watched the fight; cries of 'Lynch the nigger!' ended when more police arrived.

accounts.label: Patrolman's account
accounts.gist: The officer said he was forced to club Brown before Brown would release his hold on Lynch, and that Brown kept stabbing Lynch in his presence.

framing.detail: The Evening World headlined 'Mob Fights to Lynch Stabber' and 'Police Reserves Use Clubs in Defense of Negro,' while also calling Brown a 'Maddened Black' and 'infuriated man'; it reported witnesses who said Brown acted in self-defense.
The Herald ran a short item under 'Two Cabmen Fight Over a "Fare" and One Will Probably Die,' mentioning the lynching cries in one sentence.
The Tribune led with 'Negro Stabs 14 Times' and put the crowd's slur in a deck, while hedging the stabbing as 'it is charged' and 'it is alleged.'
The Savannah Morning News reprinted the Commercial-Advertiser story two weeks later as 'Street Row Near Police,' keeping its 'Do the nigger up!' and 'Lynch the nigger!' cries.

versions.value: Crowd rushed Brown after he was disarmed; reserves surrounded him and fought the crowd off, helped by the ambulance's arrival
Men shouted 'Lynch the nigger!' but the arrival of more police stopped the shouts and the crowd dispersed

conflicts.note: A1 is the only report of a rush and a fight with police; the others report shouts only. A1 is the earliest and most detailed on the crowd, but no other paper confirms the rush.
A3 and A4 share one text, so the 'two hundred' figure rests on two independent reports (A2, A3).

Brown accused Lynch of unfair methods in taking a fare and the men came to blows

conflicts.note: All accounts agree Brown was losing the fistfight when the knife was drawn (A1, A3, A4).
